title: The Tarasque of Noves
originLocation: Noves, Bouches-du-Rhône, Provence, France
medium: Carved local limestone freestanding sculpture
creator: Unknown Celto-Ligurian sculptor
repository: Musée Calvet (Musée Lapidaire), Avignon
anatomy: scaly dorsum and ribbed leonine chest
gaping wolf-like jaws crushing a human arm
taloned forepaws resting on two bearded severed heads
description: Unearthed in 1849 near Tarascon in southern Gaul, this menacing Iron Age limestone beast sits on its haunches with a human limb protruding from its toothed maw while resting massive clawed paws atop two bearded, closed-eyed severed heads. Combining a scaly reptilian back with lupine-leonine jaws, the pre-Roman monument embodies the Celto-Ligurian cult of death and foreshadows the medieval Provençal legend of the river-monster Tarasque.

title: Antlered Cernunnos and the Ram-Headed Serpent on the Gundestrup Cauldron
originLocation: Deposited at Rævemose bog near Gundestrup, Himmerland, Jutland, Denmark
medium: Gilded silver repoussé interior vessel plate
creator: Unknown Thraco-Celtic silversmiths
repository: National Museum of Denmark (Nationalmuseet), Copenhagen
anatomy: branching stag antlers sprouting from human crown
coiled serpent bearing curved ram horns
cross-legged lord of beasts gripping a braided torc
description: Interior Plate A of the disassembled gilded-silver Gundestrup Cauldron depicts the stag-antlered deity usually identified as Cernunnos seated cross-legged as Master of Animals amidst wolves, stags, lions, and a dolphin-rider. In his right hand he elevates a Celtic neck-torc, while his left fist grasps a fierce ram-horned serpent—a signature hybrid guardian of Gallic and Danubian sanctuary iconography.

title: Interlace Beasts and Wolf-Flanked Figures on the Sutton Hoo Mound 1 Purse Lid
originLocation: Mound 1 Ship Burial, Sutton Hoo, Suffolk, England
medium: Gold, garnet cloisonné, and millefiori glass mounted on whalebone
creator: Master goldsmith of the East Anglian royal workshop
repository: British Museum, London
anatomy: elongated ribbon-bodied beasts with interlocking jaws and limbs
raptor-like hooked beaks seizing duck-like prey
heraldic wolf-monsters devouring or whispering into a human figure's ears
description: Recovered from the princely ship burial of Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo, this opulent purse lid features seven gold-and-garnet cloisonné plaques displaying Salin Style II zoomorphic interlace. Flanking central eagles seizing waterfowl are symmetrical plaques of a standing warrior-deity gripped between two rearing lupine monsters, alongside upper mounts whose sinuous, ribbon-limbed beasts twist into intricate Germanic knotwork.

title: Insular Winged Evangelist Beasts in the Book of Kells (Folio 27v)
originLocation: Abbey of Iona, Inner Hebrides, Scotland (completed or housed at Kells, County Meath, Ireland)
medium: Insular pigments (orpiment, woad, kermes, verdigris) and iron-gall ink on calfskin vellum
creator: Columban monastic scriptorium illuminators
repository: Trinity College Library, Dublin (MS 58, Folio 27v)
anatomy: multi-winged apocalyptic lion, calf, eagle, and angel framed in cruciform compartments
stylized zoomorphic pelts patterned with Celtic spiral, trumpet, and key ornament
haloed heads and interlaced pinions fusing Ezekiel's vision with Insular knotwork
description: Divided into four compartments by an intricate stepped cross on Folio 27v of the Book of Kells, the four apocalyptic Living Creatures of Ezekiel and Revelation—winged man, winged lion, winged calf, and eagle—hover in heraldic Insular splendor. Rather than naturalistic anatomy, the Columban monks transform the sacred beasts' bodies into shimmering planes of geometric fretwork, peacock-hued feathers, and spiraling interlace.

title: The Pictish Beast on the Maiden Stone
originLocation: Chapel of Garioch, near Inverurie, Aberdeenshire, Scotland
medium: Relief-carved pink granite Class II cross-slab
creator: Unknown Pictish master mason
repository: In situ at Chapel of Garioch, Aberdeenshire (Historic Environment Scotland)
anatomy: elongated curving dolphin-like snout or trunk
sweeping crest-scroll trailing behind the head
curled spiral flipper-feet suggesting aquatic propulsion
description: Dominating the uppermost panel on the reverse of Aberdeenshire's red-granite Maiden Stone is a crisp relief of the enigmatic 'Pictish Beast,' the single most frequent zoomorphic symbol across early medieval Pictland. Characterized by a long tubular snout, a backward-sweeping head lappet, and scrolled limbs folded beneath an arched body, the creature has been interpreted as a mythic sea-kelpie, stylized cetacean, or Insular memory of classical sea-monsters.

title: Carved Dragon-Beast Head Post from the Oseberg Ship Burial
originLocation: Oseberg Burial Mound, Slagen, Vestfold, Norway
medium: Deep-relief carved maple wood with silver rivet details
creator: The Academician or Baroque Master of the Oseberg workshop
repository: Museum of the Viking Age (Kulturhistorisk museum), Oslo
commonsFile: Oslo Norway, Viking Ship Museum- Animal Head Post 9C - 21203986061.jpg
anatomy: snarling fanged jaws with bared canines
bulging round eyes above a curving draconic neck
dense surface skin composed of writhing gripping-beast interlace
description: Five ritual wooden animal-head posts accompanied two high-ranking women buried inside the oak Oseberg longship in 834 CE, likely carried in ceremonial processions to ward off malevolent spirits. Carved in maple wood, the ferocious roaring head surges from an arched neck entirely blanketed in interlocking Oseberg-style gripping beasts whose tiny paws clutch neighboring necks and borders.

title: Odin Riding the Eight-Legged Stallion Sleipnir on the Tjängvide Image Stone
originLocation: Tjängvide, Alskog parish, Gotland, Sweden
medium: Low-relief carved limestone picture stone
creator: Unknown Gotlandic stone-carver
repository: Swedish History Museum (Historiska museet), Stockholm
anatomy: eight striding equine legs arranged in paired fore and hind sets
arched stallion neck and flowing tail
supernatural gait crossing between the living world and Valhalla
description: In the upper register of the keyhole-shaped limestone picture stone from Tjängvide on Gotland, a mounted rider enters Valhalla atop Sleipnir, the shamanic eight-legged steed sired by the shape-shifted Loki for Odin. A Valkyrie bearing a drinking horn greets the horse and rider above a sailed Viking longship, rendering in stone the otherworldly mount praised in the Eddas as the swiftest of all horses across sky, sea, and Hel.

title: Víðarr Rending the Jaws of the Wolf Fenrir on the Gosforth Cross
originLocation: St Mary's Churchyard, Gosforth, Cumbria, England
medium: Relief-carved red Permian sandstone high cross
creator: Unknown Anglo-Scandinavian sculptor (the Gosforth Master)
repository: In situ at St Mary's Churchyard, Gosforth, Cumbria
anatomy: monstrous split wolf-dragon jaws stretched wide
plaited serpentine body merging into Borre-style ring-chain
forked tongue and fangs pinned by Víðarr's booted foot and spear
description: Towering 4.4 meters in a Cumbrian churchyard, the Gosforth Cross synthesizes Christian Crucifixion imagery with apocalyptic scenes from Norse Ragnarök. On its east face, Odin's silent son Víðarr braces his heavy boot against the lower jaw of the monstrous, ring-plaited wolf-serpent Fenrir while prying its upper jaw apart with his hand and spear to avenge his father's death.

title: Sigurd Piercing the Dragon Fafnir on the Ramsund Carving (Sö 101)
originLocation: Ramsundsberget, Jäder parish, Eskilstuna, Södermanland, Sweden
medium: Incised flat gneiss bedrock outcrop
creator: Commissioned by Sigridr, mother of Alríkr, in memory of Holmgeirr
repository: In situ at Ramsundsberget, Södermanland, Sweden
anatomy: colossal ribbon-like serpentine body inscribed with Younger Futhark runes
curled draconic snout and lappet framing the narrative field
underbelly pierced from below by Sigurd's sword Gram
description: Spanning nearly five meters across a glaciated granite-gneiss outcrop in Södermanland, the Ramsund carving frames the Völsung legend inside the sinuous rune-inscribed body of the hoard-guarding dragon Fafnir. From outside the serpent band, the hero Sigurd thrusts his sword Gram straight up through Fafnir's belly, while inside the coil he roasts the dragon's heart, tastes its blood, and learns the warning speech of birds.

title: Thor Fishing for the Midgard Serpent Jörmungandr on the Altuna Runestone (U 1161)
originLocation: Altuna Church, Enköping, Uppland, Sweden
medium: Incised granite runestone
creator: Runemasters Balle and Freysteinn
repository: Altuna Churchyard, Uppland, Sweden
anatomy: coiled abyssal sea-serpent body writhing beneath the waves
predatory head striking at an ox-head bait on a fishing line
cresting tendrils and jaws confronting Thor's raised hammer Mjölnir
description: Signed by the runemaster Balle on a narrow face of the Altuna Runestone, this vivid mythic scene illustrates the Eddic lay Hymiskviða, in which Thor rows into the deep ocean to hook the world-encircling Midgard Serpent Jörmungandr. So violent is the tug-of-war with the coiled sea-monster snapping at the ox-head bait below that Thor's braced foot smashes clean through the wooden hull of his boat as he raises his hammer Mjölnir.

title: The 'Urnes Beast' (Níðhöggr) and Intertwined Serpents of Urnes Stave Church
originLocation: Urnes Stave Church, Luster, Sogn og Fjordane (Vestland), Norway
medium: High-relief carved pinewood north portal
creator: Unknown master woodcarver of the Urnes style
repository: In situ at Urnes Stave Church, Luster, Norway
anatomy: slender quadruped body with swelling chest and tapering waist
almond-shaped eye extending forward to the snout
figure-eight loops of biting ribbon-serpents and tendril-dragons
description: Reused from an earlier eleventh-century timber church and set into the north wall of Urnes Stave Church, this keyhole portal defines the final, aristocratic phase of Viking animal ornament. At the base of the left jamb, a great four-legged creature—interpreted alternately as the cosmic dragon Níðhöggr gnawing Yggdrasil or a Christological lion—bites the neck of a coiling, winged serpent amid an upward cascade of writhing snakes.

title: The Pisa Griffin (Monumental Bronze Roof Guardian of Pisa Cathedral)
civilization: Medieval Pisan / Western Mediterranean Islamic-Christian Exchange
originLocation: Cast in Taifa Al-Andalus or Sicily; mounted atop Pisa Cathedral apse, Italy
medium: Cast bronze with chased plumage, roundels, and Kufic inscription
creator: Unknown Mediterranean Islamic bronze-caster; recontextualized by the Republic of Pisa
repository: Museo dell'Opera del Duomo, Pisa
anatomy: raptor head with upright equine ears and hooked eagle beak
riveted bronze wings engraved with stylized scale-feathers
muscular lion haunches incised with eagle-and-lion roundels
description: Standing over a meter tall, this monumental cast-bronze griffin was brought to Italy as maritime war booty or diplomatic tribute by the Republic of Pisa and hoisted atop the eastern gable of Pisa Cathedral for eight centuries as a civic talisman. Fitted internally with a resonance chamber that may once have emitted wind-driven roars, its hybrid eagle-and-lion body marries Islamic Kufic benedictions with Romanesque cathedral display.

title: The Golden Wyvern Standard of Wessex on the Bayeux Tapestry
originLocation: Probably embroidered in Canterbury, Kent, England, for Bishop Odo of Bayeux
medium: Crewels of dyed woollen yarn embroidered on tabby-woven linen
creator: Anglo-Saxon embroidery workshop (commissioned by Odo, Bishop of Bayeux)
repository: Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux, Bayeux, Normandy, France
commonsFile: Dragon banner - Harold Rex interfectus est.jpg
anatomy: two-legged draconic body distinct from four-legged dragons
feathered avian wings raised above a scaly torso
coiling serpentine tail and gaping fanged jaws
description: In Scene 57 of the 70-meter Bayeux Tapestry—just beside the fatal inscription 'Hic Harold Rex interfectus est'—King Harold Godwinson's standard-bearer falls clutching a three-dimensional windsock banner shaped as a winged, two-legged wyvern. Echoing the swarms of confronted wyverns, griffins, and centaurs embroidered throughout the tapestry's upper and lower borders, the standard preserves the royal Anglo-Saxon battle dragon in eleventh-century needlework.

title: Twin-Tailed Siren (Sirena Bicaudata) on a Romanesque Capital from Aguilar de Campoo
originLocation: Monasterio de Santa María la Real, Aguilar de Campoo, Palencia, Spain
medium: Deeply undercut carved limestone engaged capital
creator: Master of Aguilar de Campoo workshop
repository: Museo Arqueológico Nacional, Madrid
commonsFile: Capitel de Sta María la Real (Aguilar de Campoo) M.A.N. 01.jpg
anatomy: crowned female upper torso with flowing hair
bifurcated scaly fish tails curving symmetrically upward
outstretched human hands grasping both tail-fins
description: Carved in high relief on the left face of a late twelfth-century limestone apse capital from the Premonstratensian abbey of Santa María la Real—paired opposite Samson wrestling the lion—a crowned mermaid splays and grips her twin scaly fish tails. Across Romanesque cloisters from Castile to Poitou, this 'sirena bicaudata' warned monastic viewers against worldly seduction while establishing the visual template later absorbed into the fairy Melusine.

title: Sigurd Slaying the Winged Dragon Fafnir on the Hylestad Stave Church Portal
originLocation: Hylestad Stave Church, Valle, Setesdal, Agder, Norway
medium: Relief-carved pinewood church portal jamb
creator: Unknown Norwegian stave-church master carver
repository: Museum of Cultural History (Historisk museum), University of Oslo
commonsFile: Hylestad I, right - Fafnir and Sigurd.jpg
anatomy: sinuous Romanesque dragon neck coiled into a medallion loop
bat-like ribbed wing and clawed reptilian foreleg
gaping fanged snout spewing foliate tendrils as Gram pierces its chest
description: On the uppermost medallion of the right portal plank salvaged from the demolished Hylestad Stave Church in Setesdal, the mail-clad hero Sigurd crouches in a pit to drive his sword diagonally through the undulating body of the dragon Fafnir. Adapting pre-Christian Eddic heroism into a Christian triumph over the primordial serpent, the carver weaves Fafnir's winged, scaly coils seamlessly into the portal's inhabited vine-scrolls.

title: The Basilisk (King of Serpents) in the Aberdeen Bestiary
originLocation: Northern or Midlands scriptorium, England
medium: Tempera pigments and burnished gold leaf on vellum (Folio 66r)
creator: Principal illuminator of the Aberdeen Bestiary
repository: University of Aberdeen Library (Univ. Lib. MS 24)
anatomy: crested rooster head with lethal gaze and hooked beak
feathered bird wings and two taloned avian legs
coiled striped serpent tail confronted by its sole mortal foe, the weasel
description: Set against burnished gold leaf on Folio 66r of the Aberdeen Bestiary, the basilisk—hailed by Pliny and Isidore as king of serpents capable of killing with its gaze or breath—appears as a hybrid of crowned cockerel and looping viper. In the miniature's dynamic composition, a lithe brown weasel, the only animal immune to the monster's venom, lunges directly at the basilisk's throat.

title: The Prophecy Bird Caladrius at the Royal Sickbed (Bestiary Royal MS 12 C XIX)
originLocation: Probably Durham or Northern England
medium: Opaque pigments, ink, and gold leaf on parchment (Folio 49r)
creator: Unknown Northern English bestiary illuminator
repository: British Library, London (Royal MS 12 C XIX)
anatomy: spotless snow-white plumage devoid of any dark feather
long slender neck and diagnostic gaze
ability to absorb mortal sickness and disperse it toward the sun
description: Perched upon the draped bed of an ailing, crowned king in British Library Royal MS 12 C XIX, the pure-white Caladrius locks eyes with the patient to prophesy and heal his illness. According to the Physiologus and medieval bestiary lore, if the sick man was fated to die the bird turned its head away, whereas if he could be saved the Caladrius drew the disease into itself and flew sunward to burn the taint away—an allegory of Christ's redemptive Passion.

title: The Unicorn Captured in the Lap of a Maiden in the Rochester Bestiary
originLocation: South-Eastern England (made for Rochester Cathedral Priory, Kent)
medium: Tempera, ink, and gold leaf on vellum (Folio 10v)
creator: Master of the Rochester Bestiary
repository: British Library, London (Royal MS 12 F XIII)
commonsFile: Unicorn hunt - British Library Royal 12 F xiii f10v (detail).jpg
anatomy: single long spiraled horn projecting from the brow
compact equine-caprine body rendered in cobalt blue
docile forelegs resting in a virgin's embrace while pierced by a hunter's spear
description: Illuminated against a diapered gold ground on Folio 10v of the Rochester Bestiary, a vivid blue unicorn lays its head submissively in the lap of a seated maiden while a mail-hooded huntsman thrusts a lance through its flank. Medieval theologians read this famous hunt—whereby a beast too swift for any hunter is pacified solely by a virgin—as a figure of Christ's Incarnation in the womb of the Virgin Mary and His earthly betrayal.

title: The Manticore in the Rochester Bestiary (Folio 24v)
originLocation: South-Eastern England (Rochester Cathedral Priory, Kent)
medium: Tempera, ink, and burnished gold leaf on vellum (Folio 24v)
creator: Master of the Rochester Bestiary
repository: British Library, London (Royal MS 12 F XIII)
commonsFile: Manticore - British Library Royal 12 F xiii f24v (detail).jpg
anatomy: bearded human face wearing a pointed Phrygian cap and triple-row grin
blood-red leonine body and clawed paws
tufted scorpion-stinger tail curved over its haunches
description: Derived ultimately from Ctesias's fifth-century BCE reports of Indian monsters, the Manticore of the Rochester Bestiary strides across a hilly green ground against shimmering gold leaf, turning a human face capped in blue toward the viewer. Described in the Latin text as possessing triple rows of teeth, grey eyes, a flute-like voice, and an insatiable appetite for human flesh, its crimson lion body is rendered with bold Gothic contour lines.

title: The Bonnacon Expelling Caustic Fiery Dung in the Rochester Bestiary
originLocation: South-Eastern England (Rochester Cathedral Priory, Kent)
medium: Tempera, ink, and gold leaf on vellum (Folio 16r)
creator: Master of the Rochester Bestiary
repository: British Library, London (Royal MS 12 F XIII)
anatomy: heavy bull torso combined with a flowing equine mane
thick ram-like horns curling inward so they cannot gore
scorching stream of corrosive dung blasted backward at pursuers
description: One of the most celebrated comic-grotesque marvels of medieval illumination, Folio 16r of the Rochester Bestiary shows the Asian bull-horse Bonnacon defending itself when cornered by mailed spearmen. Because its inward-curling horns are useless for fighting, the scarlet beast unleashes a fiery, three-acre barrage of caustic dung that forces an armored hunter to recoil behind his heraldic shield.

title: The Swivel-Horned Yale (Eale) in the Rochester Bestiary
originLocation: South-Eastern England (Rochester Cathedral Priory, Kent)
medium: Tempera, ink, and gold leaf on vellum (Folio 27r)
creator: Master of the Rochester Bestiary
repository: British Library, London (Royal MS 12 F XIII)
anatomy: enormous independently swiveling horns—one extended forward, one folded back
horse-sized body with cloven hooves and boar-like jowls
tufted elephantine tail
description: Framed in red and blue against gold leaf in the Rochester Bestiary, the Ethiopian Eale—ancestor of the Tudor royal heraldic Yale—displays its defining anatomical marvel: long, articulated horns that are not fixed to the skull. When fighting, the beast thrusts one horn forward while folding the other backward in reserve so that if the leading horn is blunted, the second can immediately rotate into battle.

title: The Two-Headed Winged Amphisbaena in Harley MS 3244
originLocation: England
medium: Tinted ink and wash on parchment (Folio 62r)
creator: Illuminator of British Library Harley MS 3244
repository: British Library, London (Harley MS 3244)
anatomy: two ferocious dragon-serpent heads—one at the neck and a second terminating the tail
feathered avian wings and two clawed feet
looping body capable of rolling in either direction like a hoop
description: In this expressive thirteenth-century English bestiary miscellany (Harley MS 3244, f. 62r), the venomous Libyan serpent Amphisbaena—born in classical myth from blood dripping off Medusa's severed head—is transformed into a winged, bipedal dragon whose tail ends in a second snapping head. As Isidore of Seville recounted, its dual heads allowed it to glide forward or backward and keep watch with glowing lamp-like eyes even through winter frost.

title: Two Fishermen Lighting a Campfire on the Island-Whale Aspidochelone
originLocation: Thérouanne or Northern France / Flanders
medium: Tempera colors, gold leaf, and ink on parchment (MS. Ludwig XV 3, Folio 89v)
creator: Franco-Flemish illuminator of the Bestiary of Hugh of Fouilloy
repository: J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles (MS. Ludwig XV 3)
commonsFile: Two Fishermen on an Aspidochelone, c. 1270 (cropped).JPG
anatomy: colossal scaled sea-monster back mistaken by mariners for a sandy island
fanged jaws luring schools of fish with sweet-smelling breath
coiled piscine tail poised to plunge ship and crew into the abyss
description: Against a patterned gold ground in a c. 1270 Franco-Flemish bestiary, mariners moor their vessel to the scaly spine of the giant whale-monster Aspidochelone, mistaking its surfacing bulk for a safe island and fanning a cooking fire with bellows upon its hide. Bestiary moralists likened the creature—which dives into the ocean depths the instant it feels the heat of the flames, dragging anchored ships down with it—to the Devil's deceptive snares.

title: Gothic Chimera Gargoyle of Amiens Cathedral
originLocation: Cathédrale Notre-Dame d'Amiens, Picardy, France
medium: Carved Picard limestone architectural waterspout
creator: Cathedral masons' lodge of Amiens
repository: In situ on Cathédrale Notre-Dame d'Amiens, France
anatomy: snarling demonic muzzle hollowed as a rainwater conduit
pointed bat-like ears with a sculpted fly resting on the right ear
crouching clawed forelimbs projecting from the cathedral cornice
description: Jutting boldly from the upper stone masonry of Amiens Cathedral—the tallest completed High Gothic nave in France—this carved limestone gargoyle channels corrosive roof runoff clear of the buttresses through its open throat. Combining apotropaic guardian magic with playful stonemason wit, including a tiny insect sculpted directly onto its pointed right ear, the hybrid monster embodies the teeming marginalia of thirteenth-century cathedral exteriors.

title: Wild Men Combating a Lion, Dragon, and Unicorn (Wild Men and Moors Tapestry)
originLocation: Strasbourg, Alsace (Upper Rhine)
medium: Tapestry weave of dyed wool weft on undyed linen warp
creator: Strasbourg tapestry workshop (commissioned for the Blümel and Zorn families)
repository: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (Inv. 54.1431)
anatomy: humanoid woodland body covered from neck to ankles in shaggy blue and ochre fur
bare hands, feet, and painted facial features
uprooted tree trunks and boulders wielded against forest beasts
description: Woven in Strasbourg around 1400 for patrician Alsatian households, this vibrant woollen frieze portrays shaggy, pelt-covered 'Wilde Leute'—untamed woodland humans living beyond feudal civilization—battling a lion, a winged dragon, and a unicorn before bringing game home to a wild woman and her children in a rocky crag. In Upper Rhenish tapestry culture, the Wild Man simultaneously embodied primal natural vigor, uncorrupted fidelity, and mastery over monstrous wilderness.

title: Winged Serpent Mélusine Hovering Above Château de Lusignan (Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry)
originLocation: Bourges or Paris, France
medium: Tempera, gold, and lapis lazuli on vellum (March calendar miniature, Folio 3v)
creator: Paul, Jean, and Herman de Limbourg (and Barthélemy d'Eyck)
repository: Musée Condé, Château de Chantilly (MS 65)
commonsFile: Les Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry mars.jpg
anatomy: golden winged dragon-serpent form taken after her Saturday bath taboo was broken
ribbons of ribbed bat-like wings against a lapis lazuli sky
guardian flight circling the Tour Poitevine of Lusignan Castle
description: High in the ultramarine sky above the white ramparts of the Château de Lusignan in the March calendar leaf of Jean de Berry's Très Riches Heures, a golden winged dragon circles the rightmost tower: the fairy ancestress Mélusine. Celebrated in Jean d'Arras's 1393 romance written for the Duke of Berry himself, Mélusine magically erected the fortress of Lusignan before her husband spied upon her serpent-tailed bath, compelling her to fly away in draconic form and return shrieking above the towers whenever the lordship changed hands.

title: Headless Blemmyes and Monstrous Marvels of Ethiopia in the Livre des merveilles du monde
originLocation: Angers, Duchy of Anjou, France
medium: Tempera and gold paint on parchment (MS M.461, Folios 26v–27r)
creator: Master of the Geneva Boccaccio (Colin d'Amiens?)
repository: The Morgan Library & Museum, New York (MS M.461)
commonsFile: Livre des merveilles du monde MS M.461, fols. 26v–27r.jpg
anatomy: headless human torso with eyes, nose, and mouth set directly into the chest
club-wielding Panotii giant with ears hanging down to the shoulders
horned giant bird of prey and cave-dwelling troglodytes
description: Across a luminous double-page landscape in the Morgan Library's Livre des merveilles du monde, the Master of the Geneva Boccaccio populates the imagined borders of Ethiopia with the 'Plinian races' inherited from classical geography and medieval mappae mundi. Prominent in the foreground stands a headless Blemmye whose facial features gaze directly out from his bare chest, flanked by a huge-eared giant, serpent-eating cave dwellers, and a horned raptor.

title: Saint Martha Taming the Man-Eating Tarasque in the Hours of Louis de Laval
originLocation: Bourges, Berry, France
medium: Tempera and liquid gold on vellum (BnF MS Latin 920, Folio 317v)
creator: Jean Colombe and workshop
repository: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (MS Latin 920)
commonsFile: Heures de Louis de Laval - BNF Lat920 f317v (Sainte Marthe et la Tarasque).jpg
anatomy: armored turtle-like carapace spiked along the spine
lion-like head devouring a human victim feet-first
six bear-like clawed legs and scaly viper tail subdued by a girdle and holy water
description: Illuminated by Jean Colombe for the Breton nobleman Louis de Laval, Folio 317v visualizes Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend account of Saint Martha subduing the amphibious monster of the Rhône at Nerluc (renamed Tarascon). Even as a half-swallowed man's legs kick from its jaws, the spiny-shelled, dragon-tailed Tarasque bows meekly on a leash while Martha sprinkles it with holy water from an aspergillum.

title: The Lady and the Unicorn: 'À mon seul désir' (La Dame à la licorne)
originLocation: Designed in Paris (Master of Anne of Brittany); woven in the Southern Netherlands
medium: Millefleurs tapestry woven in wool and silk
creator: Cartoons attributed to Jean d'Ypres (Master of Anne of Brittany); Brussels or Bruges weavers
repository: Musée de Cluny – Musée national du Moyen Âge, Paris
commonsFile: Tapisserie de la Dame à la Licorne (Musée de Cluny, Paris).jpg
anatomy: slender white equine-caprine body with cloven hooves
long straight spiraled ivory horn and silken goat-beard
heraldic posture bearing the crescents of the Le Viste coat of arms
description: Crowning a celebrated six-tapestry cycle of the Five Senses woven for the Lyon magistrate Jean IV Le Viste, 'À mon seul désir' stages a noblewoman placing her jewel necklace into a casket before a blue damask pavilion held open by a heraldic lion and a snow-white unicorn. Against a vermilion millefleurs ground teeming with rabbits, birds, and wildflowers, the cloven-hoofed, goat-bearded unicorn embodies courtly chivalry and spiritual purity.

title: The Unicorn in Captivity (from The Hunt of the Unicorn Tapestries)
originLocation: Designed in Paris; woven in the Southern Netherlands (probably Brussels)
medium: Wool warp with wool, silk, silver, and gilt-wrapped thread weft
creator: Parisian cartoonist (circle of Jean d'Ypres) and Southern Netherlandish weavers
repository: The Met Cloisters, Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (37.80.6)
commonsFile: The Unicorn in Captivity - Google Art Project.jpg
anatomy: snow-white stallion-goat hybrid with tufted fetlocks and cloven hooves
long twisted horn rising from the center of the forehead
flanks flecked with ruby pomegranate juice beneath a golden collar and chain
description: Perhaps the single most iconic textile of the European Middle Ages, the final panel of the Cloisters' Unicorn Tapestries depicts the resurrected or willingly tamed unicorn resting inside a low gilded wooden paddock tethered loosely to a fruit-laden pomegranate tree. Surrounded by more than eighty identifiable botanical species woven in dyed wool, silk, and metallic threads, the radiant beast simultaneously evokes Christ risen in paradise and the bridegroom bound in courtly marriage.
